character_and_relationship_context: Niran Wong formerly worked as a senior accountant for the Ministry of Finance in Bangkok, a post held for thirty-seven years. Their office overlooked a courtyard where jasmine vines crept over trellises, and the afternoon heat pressed against the windows until the air conditioning hummed with the effort. Colleagues knew Niran as meticulous and reserved, the one who caught rounding errors before reports went to the deputy director. Niran took pride in that quiet reputation for accuracy, for never being wrong. Niran's only child, a geotechnical engineer, accepted a position in Calgary, and after a year of video calls and time-zone calculations, Niran retired early, sold the family home in Thon Buri, and moved with two suitcases and a small wooden Buddha. At the distribution centre, Niran works the night shift starting at 11 p.m., moving through the aisles with unhurried precision. The floor is stained concrete and the air is a constant five degrees Celsius even in July. Most of the night crew are young—students, part-timers, new immigrants from the Philippines and Somalia. They call Niran 'Auntie' or 'Uncle' uncertainly, unsure of the pronouns Niran prefers; Niran simply says 'Niran' and lets the confusion sit. Loyalty to family comes before loyalty to labels; Niran's child calls them 'Por' in private, and that is enough. On break, Niran sips black tea from a thermos while others scroll through phones. Sometimes a co-worker asks about Thailand, and Niran answers with a fact: 'The mangoes are sweeter there.' Niran never mentions loneliness. Duty is the architecture of Niran's life: duty to their daughter, which is why Niran endures the cold and the 11 p.m. start time; duty to their supervisors, which is why Niran never leaves a pallet unstraightened; and duty to themselves, which means Niran cannot complain—complaining would imply regret, and Niran does not regret the choice. Still, a tension exists: the same order that soothes Niran also isolates them. In Bangkok, order was shared—everyone in the office knew the filing system. Here, the precision is solitary. No one else notices when a pallet is stacked with thirty-two boxes instead of thirty-three; only Niran knows why it matters. At 6:30 a.m., the fluorescent lights flicker off, and Niran logs out and walks to the bus stop under a pale winter sky. Niran thinks of the ledger left behind, columns of numbers that never argued back, and then of their daughter's laugh over dinner last Sunday. The cold bites, but Niran does not pull up their collar. Duty requires endurance, and endurance, Niran has learned, is a kind of love. In relation to the former colleague, they were lunch companions in the ministry courtyard, but conversations never strayed beyond work and polite topics. They exchanged farewells at Niran's retirement party, with no promises to keep in touch. Niran knows the colleague still works in Bangkok; their paths diverged cleanly when Niran left. Since moving to Calgary, Niran has not initiated contact with any former colleagues, focusing instead on family and the new job. On breaks at the distribution centre, Niran typically sits alone and does not seek conversation. In Bangkok, Niran maintained friendly but bounded work relationships, never extending them beyond office hours.
objective_situation: It is 2 a.m. during Niran's break. Niran's phone buzzes with a message from a former colleague in Bangkok, a man Niran once shared quiet lunches with in the ministry courtyard. The message says: 'I will be in Calgary for a conference next week. Can we have dinner? It has been too long.' Niran stares at the message, thumb hovering. Niran has not spoken to this colleague since leaving Thailand. The break room is empty, and the tea in Niran's thermos is growing cold.
state_and_available_memories: Niran is midway through a night shift, physically tired but alert, with a body acclimated to the 2 a.m. break routine. The empty break room feels quieter than usual, and the tea in the thermos has gone lukewarm. Niran has been thinking of nothing in particular, just the ambient hum of the warehouse. Immediately available memories are triggered by reading the message: Niran recalls the jasmine-scented courtyard and the colleague's habit of ordering khao man gai every lunch. Niran remembers the colleague's sincere toast at the retirement party and the slight awkwardness of saying goodbye. The name on the screen brings back the precise weight of the ministry's afternoon heat against the window.
name: Niran Wong
